newsitem.title: GERMANY: BMW worries about Rover profit timetable.
newsitem.headline: BMW worries about Rover profit timetable.

text.p: Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW) Chairman Bernd Pischetsrieder said on Monday that its British unit Rover Group may fail to turn a profit by 2000 as BMW has long hoped it would.

Pischetsrieder said in an interview with Handelsblatt newspaper that Rover, which has lost money ever since BMW bought it in 1994, was being hit hard by the strength of the pound which made it harder to export.
"If the British currency remains so strong, it could become more difficult to hit the black at Rover as planned, especially when taking into account that Rover is expected to boost exports," he said.
The pound, which has risen nearly 12 percent against the mark this year to around 2.92, makes it harder to sell Rover vehicles abroad by making them cost more in foreign currencies.

Pischetsrieder had originally laid out a timetable for Rover that included it turning a profit by 2000 and has seen hundres of millions of marks poured into the company in an attempt to make it more competitive.
The British car company had appeared to be on line to meet Pischetsrieder's forecasts, triming costs and boosting sales.
Rover posted a 279 million mark ($153.6 million) pre-tax loss on ordinary business activities in 1996, down from a 335 million marks loss the year before.

Pischetsrieder has occasionally been criticised for pouring funds into Rover and rumours have circulated of late that Rover was on the sales block, including one report that Chrysler Corp was interested in the company.
But far from backing away from the company, BMW has taken firmer control over the unit, moving leading executives from Munich to the UK.
Although Rover's Land Rover and Range Rover models have sold well, the company's car models have faced quality problems and been priced too high, analysts said.
Indeed, the strength of the pound comes at a bad time for Rover with the company trying to move beyond its home market and expand sales overseas.
More than 55 percent of Rover's overall sales were acheived outside the UK. Turnover climbed five percent in first half of this year to 250,382 units.
